newsitem.title: USA: Wired updates HotWired site, aims at Web community.
newsitem.headline: Wired updates HotWired site, aims at Web community.

text.p: Wired Ventures Inc., aiming to provide a new interactive experience to members of its digital community, is launching a revamped version of its HotWired site on the World Wide Web.

The new site, due to go live on Tuesday, is designed to enable members to experience pages that come alive with theatrical motion and interactivity, encouraging them to take an active role in the emerging digital culture of the Internet as well as keeping current on Web issues.

"At the highest level, the redesign is oriented towards making people regular visitors of HotWired, to get them to burrow more deeply (into the site)," said Hunter Madsen, vice president of marketing at HotWired.

The new site reflects the hip approach of the company's other major media property, Wired magazine, which since its launch in 1993 has sought to establish itself as the chronicle of the emerging digital age.
Editors at Wired Digital Inc., the company's online media division, which developed HotWired 4.0, have geared the updated site to help people become insiders in the new and fast-paced medium.
HotWired 4.0 is centered around six sections, including its Webmonkey how-to guide for Web junkies, which provides tutorials, tricks and tools for both novice and professional Web developers.

HotWired is merging its commentary on society, politics and culture by combining elements of its Netizen, Packet and Brain Tennis into a section called Synapse to include writers like media critic Jon Katz.

The site will also include a section on Dream Jobs, culled from the net, a music, video and chat "Beta Lounge" on Thursdays, and RGB Gallery, a Web-based digital art gallery spotlighting multimedia works of art created exclusively for HotWired's Internet site.
A sixth section, Net Surf, offers Suck.com co-founder Joey Anuff' daily picks and pans of the Web, as well as pointers to live Web events, conferences and sites.
Madsen said initial advertising space is sold out, including sponsorships from such major advertisers as General Motors Corp.'s Oldsmobile division.
The site will be visible at the company's site at (www.hotwired.com) from Tuesday, executives said.

The overhaul of the HotWired site aims to boost Wired's profile among its more than 600,000 existing members and to attract more participants from the tens of millions of people who have access to the Internet.
Madsen estimates HotWired could double or triple its membership simply by tracking the growth in the number of Internet users, which could hit 100 million next year.

HotWired was first launched in October 1994 and was an early innovator in bringing advertising to the World Wide Web by introducing banner advertisements, which are hyperlinked to direct the viewer to an advertiser's site.

Banner advertisements have since become widely accepted on the Internet, and HotWired plans to continue to innovate on the adverting front and build its Web presence, with one other site now under development.

HotWired executives declined to discuss financial targets for the site or recent results, but said their goal was to push the envelope by demonstrating leading edge content and developing a community on its site.

"The Web is really difficult in terms of media -- with brutal standards of success," said June Cohen, senior producer of the site. "If we were just putting a magazine on the Web, that's just missing the point."
The site uses dynamic HTML, a new version of Hypertext Markup Language that enables sophisticated interactive multimedia features to be used without having to download additional plug-ins.
